name: Caffeine pre-workout
lead: Pre-workout supplements are multi-ingredient powders, capsules or drinks taken before training to increase energy, focus and endurance; caffeine is their near-universal base, found in 86% of bestselling products in one analysis [1]. Other typical ingredients include creatine, beta-alanine, citrulline, amino acids and nitrates [1][2].

Caffeine itself is described as a proven ergogenic aid at moderate doses, with documented improvements in sprint, endurance and strength outcomes [3]. Evidence for the other blend ingredients is mixed, and doses in commercial products are often below those studied [1][2]. Regulators have acted against some stimulants sold in the category, such as ephedrine (2004) and DMAA (2012) [1].
infobox: Caffeine; Grokipedia cites about 200 to 300 mg per serving [2]
Dietary supplement; FDA does not pre-approve [1]

paras: Dan Duchaine formulated Ultimate Orange in 1982 in Venice, California; it contained ephedra [1]. After ephedra-linked adverse events, the FDA banned ephedrine in supplements in 2004 [1]. Patrick Arnold formulated a DMAA product in 2005, and the FDA acted against DMAA in 2012 after cardiovascular reports [1]. The market grew from about 2.7 billion US dollars in 2008 to about 14.2 billion in 2022 [1].

Caffeine is a non-selective adenosine receptor antagonist, with A2A receptors central to its wakefulness effects; it also inhibits phosphodiesterase and affects dopamine signalling [3]. Onset is roughly 45 to 60 minutes and peak levels occur within 1 to 2 hours; it is metabolised mainly by CYP1A2 [3].

Wikipedia describes moderate caffeine intake as improving sprinting, time trials, endurance, power and muscular strength, and lowering perceived exertion [3]. Reviews cited in Grokipedia attribute pre-workout benefits mainly to well-dosed caffeine and beta-alanine rather than blend synergy [2]. Users often report feeling more energised, but Wikipedia notes there is little quantitative proof of the subjective effect [1].

Common effects of caffeine include anxiety, jitteriness and insomnia, with anxiety more likely above roughly 300 to 400 mg [3]. Energy-drink-level intakes of about 320 mg have been linked to short-term blood-pressure and palpitation effects [3]. Health Canada advises a maximum of 400 mg per day for healthy adults [3]. Pre-workouts can also contain stimulants such as synephrine and higenamine linked to cardiovascular risk, and ingredient accuracy and contamination have been reported as problems [1]. The FDA lacks the resources to test supplements before sale [1].

Registered trials have studied caffeinated versus non-caffeinated pre-workout on resistance exercise performance (24 participants) [4], multi-ingredient pre-workout and energy expenditure during running [5], and caffeine-based supplement effects on muscle power [6]. All are small (12 to 36 participants), and outcomes are performance measures, not changes in physical appearance.

timeline.event: Ultimate Orange, regarded as the first pre-workout, is formulated [1].

card.summary: Stimulant-based training powders; caffeine is the best-supported ingredient and the rest is mixed.
card.note: High stimulant loads can raise blood pressure and cause anxiety and insomnia.

quick.overview:
Pre-workouts are powders taken before the gym, built around caffeine plus ingredients such as creatine, beta-alanine and citrulline.

Caffeine has well-documented effects on exercise performance. Evidence for other ingredients is mixed, and the benefit relates to training, not facial or body aesthetics directly.
quick.mechanism: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, raising alertness and lowering perceived effort.
quick.risks: Anxiety, insomnia and raised blood pressure are documented; ingredient accuracy varies and banned stimulants (ephedrine, DMAA) have appeared in the category.
